analysis.one_liner: Lets every phone user join the Do Not Call list and sue robocallers $500 per illegal call.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the House on April 15, 2026 and referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no markup, no vote, and just 2 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would expand federal Do Not Call protections so they cover every phone subscriber, not just people with home landlines. It would strip out the allowance that lets a company call someone on the list once every 12 months without penalty, so any call to a listed number would count as a violation carrying $500 in statutory damages. It would also broaden the definition of an "automatic telephone dialing system" so that machines dialing from a list of numbers count as robocallers, closing a path companies use to argue their dialers are not covered.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone with a phone who is tired of unwanted sales, scam, and debt-collection calls. Cell phone users, who are currently outside the Do Not Call rules because the law only protects 'residential' lines, would gain the most: they could register for the list, and calls to them in violation would carry a private right of action with $500 in statutory damages per call, doubled or tripled if a court finds the violation was willful or knowing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Every phone user, especially cell phone owners

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes the word 'residential' from the Do Not Call rules, so the list and its protections would cover all telephone subscribers, including cell phone and VoIP users, who today fall outside the definition.

It removes the provision that lets a caller make 'more than one telephone call within any 12-month period' to a listed subscriber without violating the rule, replacing it with 'a telephone call' — so a single unwanted call to a listed number would be a violation, and it strikes the 'up to' qualifier on the statutory damages figure.

It expands the private right of action to match the broadened rules, letting individuals sue callers who violate the Do Not Call requirements directly rather than relying only on FCC or FTC enforcement.

It rewrites the definition of 'automatic telephone dialing system' to include equipment dialing 'a list of telephone numbers' successively 'without human intervention', covering list-based auto-dialers that currently escape the robocall rules because they do not dial random or sequential numbers.
The FCC would have 270 days after enactment to rewrite its regulations to implement the expanded rules.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that profit from high-volume outbound calling: telemarketers, debt collectors, lead generators, and the firms that sell them dialing technology. They would face per-call lawsuits from consumers and would need to scrub calling lists more aggressively or drop automated calling to listed numbers entirely. Some of that compliance cost could be passed along in prices, and the broadened dialer definition could sweep in ordinary business texting and calling tools.
analysis.who_pays_short: Telemarketers, debt collectors, and dialer vendors

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection: removing the once-per-12-months allowance and keeping a $500 per-call private right of action creates heavy litigation exposure for legitimate businesses, not just scam operations — a single miskept list could generate thousands of lawsuits, and those costs are partly passed to consumers.

The broadened definition of an automatic dialing system would cover equipment that dials from stored lists without human intervention, which reaches beyond classic robocallers into widely used customer-contact and texting software that legitimate businesses and nonprofits rely on.

Honest supporters would acknowledge that Do Not Call registration has limited effect on the worst callers — outright scammers already ignore the rules — so the bill's biggest practical gain is giving private litigants a tool against them, at the cost of the litigation burden above.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is real: cell phone users, who receive most of today's spam and scam calls, would finally be covered by the Do Not Call list with a per-call lawsuit remedy. The cost is that the per-call damages structure, with no safe harbor for a first call, puts genuine litigation risk on any large outbound caller that makes a list error. A balanced version would pair the expanded coverage with a tiered penalty for first offenses. As written, the enforcement tool is strong and the exposure is broad — a tradeoff that favors consumers over calling businesses.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which has not scheduled any action on it, so it sits there while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Representative Janice Schakowsky introduced the bill in the House on April 15, 2026, with one original cosponsor.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, the committee with jurisdiction over telephone law.
The action history shows no further steps since the referral — no subcommittee hearing, no markup, no floor scheduling.
The bill has 2 cosponsors, both House Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody has lost anything yet, because the bill has not advanced or failed. To the extent there is a status quo winner, it is the outbound-calling industry — telemarketers, debt collectors, and dialer vendors — which remains free of the new liability because the bill has not moved.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred; so far every sponsor and cosponsor is a House Democrat (2 cosponsors of 217), and no Republican has signed on.

industries.note: These businesses make money by calling consumers, including people on the Do Not Call list who currently tolerate one call per entity per year. The bill would make any call to a listed subscriber a violation carrying $500 per call in statutory damages, and would extend the list to cover cell phones, their largest contact channel.

Debt collectors rely heavily on automated dialers to reach consumers, and they are frequent targets of telephone-law lawsuits. A broader dialer definition plus a per-call private right of action with no once-a-year allowance would sharply raise their litigation risk.

Their products dial from stored customer lists without human intervention, which the bill's rewritten definition would classify as automatic telephone dialing systems, exposing their customers to the robocall rules. Vendors would face pressure to redesign equipment or lose sales to regulated users.

industries.industry: Lead generators and marketing data brokers
industries.note: They sell consumer phone lists to callers; a per-call damages regime covering every subscriber makes bad or recycled lists far more expensive, shrinking demand for their product.

analysis.trajectory: With 2 cosponsors, no hearing, and no committee action since the April referral, the bill looks like most private-member consumer bills: it will probably die in committee when this Congress ends unless the Energy and Commerce Committee elevates robocall enforcement to a priority. Broadening it beyond two sponsors would be the first sign of movement.
